passage: "Okay, Sumit, just listen to this draft and tell me it's fine." Mridul held up his phone. "'Hey, I'm sorry if you felt let down about Saturday. Traffic was insane and work has been crazy, you know how it is.'" He looked up. "Good, right? Short. Friendly." Sumit didn't say anything. Mridul scrolled, frowning. "I mean, it's true. There was traffic. Sort of. Okay, I left late because I stayed at Karan's thing. But Rhea doesn't need all that detail. I just want this weird feeling to go away, and for us to be normal again." He paused, thumb over the send button. "So why does it feel wrong?"

qa.q: Why did Mridul actually leave late?
qa.a: He left late because he stayed at Karan's thing.

qa.q: What does Mridul really want from sending the draft?
qa.a: He feels uneasy and wants that weird feeling to go away and things to be normal again, without facing that he was wrong.

qa.q: What could Mridul change in the draft?
qa.a: He could drop "if you felt" and the traffic excuse, and say plainly that he chose Karan's event and let Rhea down.

qa.q: How might Rhea read "I'm sorry if you felt let down"?
qa.a: Rhea would likely hear it as questioning Rhea's feelings instead of owning the act, which could hurt more than no message.

grounding: Shows a young man drafting an 'I'm sorry if you felt' message with traffic and work excuses, wanting forgiveness without the discomfort of being wrong.

passage: I'm Nilesh, Tarun's roommate, and I watched him write the same message for forty minutes last night. He'd skipped his friend Anjali's farewell dinner to go to a gaming tournament. I heard the draft, because he reads everything aloud. "Sorry if you felt hurt, the office kept me back and the roads were jammed." The office didn't keep him back. He was right here on the sofa with me at seven. He'd type, delete, sigh, type again. At one point he said, "I just want her to not be mad." He didn't say, "I want to make it right." I don't know what he finally sent. But he looked more uncomfortable after sending it than before.

qa.q: Where was Tarun at seven, according to Nilesh?
qa.a: He was right here on the sofa with Nilesh at seven.

qa.q: What does "I just want her to not be mad" suggest about Tarun's aim?
qa.a: It suggests he mainly wants to escape the discomfort, not to own what he did or make it right.

qa.q: What would a better message from Tarun include?
qa.a: The truth, that he chose the tournament over Anjali's farewell, and a plain sorry without "if you felt" or invented excuses.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel if she later learns the office excuse wasn't true?
qa.a: Anjali would likely feel hurt twice over, first by the missed farewell and then by being given a false reason.

grounding: Shows, through a roommate's eyes, a young man drafting an excuse-filled 'sorry if you felt' message to be forgiven without facing being wrong.

passage:
"Read this," said Omkar, pushing his phone across to Shankar in the hostel room. "Is it okay?"
Shankar read aloud: "'Hey Nandini, I'm sorry if you felt bad about Saturday. The traffic was insane and then work stuff came up. You know how it is.'" He looked up. "You missed her exhibition."
"I know. That's why I'm apologising."
"You're not, though. 'Sorry if you felt' means sorry she's upset, not sorry you didn't show up."
"But there was traffic!"
"For three hours?"
Omkar grabbed his phone back. "I just want this to be over."
"She'll hear that," said Shankar.

qa.q: What did Omkar miss on Saturday?
qa.a: Nandini's exhibition.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling as he wrote the draft?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and defensive, wanting to be forgiven quickly without admitting he was wrong.

qa.q: What turning point does Shankar offer?
qa.a: Shankar points out that "sorry if you felt" is not a real apology, giving Omkar a chance to own that he didn't show up instead of blaming traffic.

qa.q: How might Nandini experience Omkar's draft if he sends it?
qa.a: She would likely feel more hurt, hearing excuses and blame rather than a real apology.

grounding: A young man drafts an apology that begins "sorry if you felt" and blames traffic, wanting forgiveness without the discomfort of being wrong.

passage:
I remember the draft I wrote to Jaya after missing her graduation dinner.
It went like this: "Hey, sorry if you felt let down. Work was crazy, my manager kept me back, and then the metro was jammed. Hope you understand."
I read it and felt better. It wasn't my fault, the message said. It was work, the manager, the metro.
Then I read it again, pretending I was Jaya. It didn't say I was sorry for anything. It said I was sorry she felt something. I'd left the office at seven, and the dinner was at eight. The metro wasn't the reason.
I'm Pradeep, and I deleted that message. I didn't want to feel wrong. But I was.

qa.q: What event did Pradeep miss?
qa.a: Jaya's graduation dinner.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he first read his draft?
qa.a: Pradeep felt better, relieved, because the message put the blame on work, the manager and the metro.

qa.q: What turning point did Pradeep reach?
qa.a: By reading the draft as if Pradeep were Jaya, the excuses became visible, and deleting it opened the way to a real apology.

qa.q: How would Jaya likely have felt reading the original draft?
qa.a: She would probably have felt more hurt and dismissed, reading excuses instead of a real apology.

grounding: A young adult recalls drafting a "sorry if you felt" apology full of excuses, then seeing it as a way to avoid feeling wrong.

passage:
Internship supervisor's note, Friday

Tushar came to my desk at lunch and asked me to check an email he'd written to his friend Aadhya. He said it was "important to get it right."
The draft began: "I'm sorry if you felt hurt that I missed your recital. The workload here has been really heavy, and traffic was terrible." He'd missed it on Wednesday.
I asked him, "Did you miss it because of traffic?" He paused. "Not really. I forgot."
I suggested that the email might land better if it said just that: that he forgot, and he's sorry. He looked uncomfortable. He said he'd think about it. I'll check in with him on Monday.

qa.q: What event had Tushar missed?
qa.a: Aadhya's recital, on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when the supervisor suggested a simpler email?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable, not wanting to feel the discomfort of being wrong.

qa.q: What turning point did the supervisor offer?
qa.a: By asking whether traffic was the real reason, the supervisor helped Tushar see the excuses and suggested an honest apology instead.

qa.q: How might Aadhya experience an honest email saying he forgot?
qa.a: She might still feel hurt, but she would likely feel more respected than if she read excuses about traffic.

grounding: A supervisor notices a young man drafting an apology full of excuses and gently suggests he own his mistake instead.

passage:
Friday night

I skipped Maria's book launch. The one she's been planning since January. I just didn't go. I was tired, I stayed in and watched a match.

Now she's messaged: "Didn't see you there." That's all.

I've been drafting for an hour. Draft 1: "I'm so sorry if you felt let down, the traffic was insane." There was no traffic. I never left the flat.

Draft 2: "Sorry, work has been crazy this week, I'm sure you understand." Also a lie.

I know why I'm doing this. I want her to say "it's okay" without me having to feel like the bad guy. But reading these back, they sound like I'm blaming the city for my choices.

She'd see through it. She always does.

Not sending anything tonight. Tomorrow I'll try one without excuses.

Imran

qa.q: When had Maria been planning the book launch since?
qa.a: She had been planning it since January.

qa.q: What does Imran want from the excuse drafts?
qa.a: Imran wants to be forgiven without feeling like the bad guy, avoiding the uncomfortable guilt of being wrong.

qa.q: What would a better message to Maria look like?
qa.a: A short, honest one: 'I didn't come, and I have no good excuse. I'm sorry I missed your big day,' without traffic or work.

qa.q: How might Maria react to the 'sorry if you felt' draft?
qa.a: Maria would probably see through it and feel more hurt, since it blames the city and her feelings instead of owning the choice.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult drafting 'sorry if you felt' excuses blaming traffic and work, wanting forgiveness without the discomfort of being wrong.
